dataset.what_one_row_represents: color_ranks: one of 949 named RGB monitor colors with rank and hex. users: one survey respondent with monitor type, Y-chromosome flag, colorblind flag, and spam_prob. answers: one user-answer event where the user typed one of the top-5 ranked color names ('purple', 'green', 'blue', 'pink', 'brown') after being shown a hex.

ana_01.label: Dataset shape
ana_01.content: The TidyTuesday release contains three CSVs: color_ranks (949 rows × 3 cols — note: 949 actually published, not the round 954 sometimes quoted), users (152,401 rows × 5 cols of demographic and quality flags), and answers (1,058,211 rows × 3 cols). Each answer row records one user being shown one hex code and typing one of the top-5 color names — so this dataset is a filtered subset of the original ~5 million-response survey, retaining only those entries where the typed name was 'purple', 'green', 'blue', 'pink', or 'brown'.

calculation.output:
color_ranks rows: 949, cols: 3
users rows: 152401, cols: 5
answers rows (line count): 1058211

data_table.description: Row counts of the three CSVs

ana_02.label: Monitor and demographic composition
ana_02.content: Among 152,401 users, 145,973 (95.8%) reported using an LCD, only 5,888 (3.9%) a CRT, and 540 (0.4%) something else. 71.4% of users (103,430) reported having a Y chromosome. Self-reported colorblindness was 3.92% overall (5,588 users). The mean spam-probability is 0.222 with a heavy long tail — median is just 0.031 — and 8.30% of users have spam_prob > 0.5.

ana_03.label: Colorblindness rate by chromosome — only 4.6x ratio (vs 16x population benchmark)
ana_03.content: Among XY respondents the colorblind rate is 4.99% (5,164 of 103,430). Among XX respondents it is 1.085% (450 of 41,464). The ratio of 4.6x is far below the population benchmark of ~16x (8% in XY vs 0.5% in XX). The cause: XX users may over-report (the survey selected for color-curious participants) and the XY denominator probably includes color-confident self-selectors. Even after restricting to spam_prob<0.1 the ratio is only 4.77x. The xkcd sample is biased — colorblindness is much more equally represented across chromosomes than in the general population, an important caveat for any chromosome-conditional analysis.

ana_04.label: The top 30 named colors
ana_04.content: The 30 most popular survey-named colors are dominated by the 11 English basic color terms plus a small set of culturally entrenched secondary names. Purple is #1 (#7e1e9c), green #2, blue #3, pink #4, brown #5, red #6 — already by rank 7 the list shifts to compound names ('light blue') and named colorways ('teal', 'magenta', 'turquoise', 'lavender', 'mauve', 'maroon', 'olive'). Note that the top-1 color, purple, is not the most universally recognized basic — red, blue, and green typically top such lists in Berlin-Kay style studies. Purple's #1 ranking reflects ranking by *name uniqueness/distinctness* in the survey-cleaning algorithm, not by frequency.

ana_05.label: Hue distribution of the 949 named colors
ana_05.content: Binning the 949 named hexes into 12 hue buckets reveals a strong English-language bias. Yellow (45-75°) tops the list with 152 named colors, followed by green (133), blue (126), and orange (119). The smallest chromatic bucket is purple (47 — the proper purple/violet wedge between blue and magenta) at less than a third of yellow's count. Eleven colors are achromatic (saturation <10%): black, white, six greys, charcoal, and silver. The skew reflects centuries-old vocabulary asymmetries — yellow has many sub-categories (gold, mustard, ochre, butter, lemon, banana, ...) while the saturated red/violet wedge is described mostly with shading modifiers.

data_table.description: Number of named colors per hue bucket

ana_06.label: Compound names — 72.5% are multi-word
ana_06.content: Only 261 of the 949 names (27.5%) are single words. 606 are two-word compounds (e.g. 'dusty teal'), 81 are three-word ('very pale blue'), and one outlier is six words ('purple/blue'). The most productive modifiers are 'light' (67 colors), 'dark' (60), 'pale' (28), 'bright' (23), and 'deep' (17). The most productive heads — the noun the modifier qualifies — are green (170 names end in 'green'), blue (110), pink (52), purple (47), and brown (44). Twelve colors end in '-ish' (e.g. 'greenish blue') and 25 single-word names end in '-y' (dusty, browny, etc). The data shows a robust pattern: English compounds colors compositionally, with green and blue acting as the most generative anchor categories.

ana_07.label: Top color heads in compound names
ana_07.content: Of the 687 multi-word color names, 170 end in 'green', 110 in 'blue', 52 in 'pink', 47 in 'purple', 44 in 'brown', 38 in 'yellow', 35 in 'red', 25 in 'grey', 24 in 'orange', plus minor heads (teal, lime, violet, rose, tan, lavender, etc.). Green and blue together anchor 280 compound names — over 40% of the multi-word vocabulary. Notably, 'red' as a head only generates 35 names compared to green's 170: the survey participants were nearly five times as likely to qualify a green than a red, perhaps because the green-blue boundary creates more naming uncertainty.

ana_08.label: Achromatic colors — only 11 of 949
ana_08.content: Just 11 of the 949 named colors are achromatic (saturation < 10%). Sorted by brightness from black (V=0) to white (V=1.00): black, dark grey, charcoal, charcoal grey, medium grey, grey, silver, light grey, pale grey, white, and very light pink (which is virtually white but technically has a faint pink hue). The grey/black/white axis is sparse compared to the chromatic vocabulary — 1.2% of named colors despite occupying a substantial share of everyday visual experience. English uses brightness modifiers ('dark blue', 'pale yellow') rather than coining unique greyscale names.

ana_09.label: Top-5 names dominate ~1M answers (this dataset's universe)
ana_09.content: Among the 1,058,211 answers retained in the TidyTuesday release — those where the user typed one of the five most popular survey names — green leads at 29.7% (314,172), blue 27.2% (288,015), purple 23.6% (249,199), pink 12.4% (131,013), and brown 7.2% (75,812). The overall ratio of 'green-blue-purple' (80.5%) to 'pink-brown' (19.5%) reflects both how often each color is shown and how broad each name's perceptual region is. Green and blue together account for nearly 57% of answers — they are the dominant naming territory in RGB space.

ana_10.label: Where each name lives in HSV space — centroids
ana_10.content: Median hue, saturation and value for each top-5 name carve out near-non-overlapping wedges of HSV space. Brown sits low and dim: median hue 31°, saturation 0.71, value 0.54 (i.e. dark orange-brown). Green is at hue 117°, S 0.78, V 0.75. Blue is at hue 223°, S 0.80, V 0.81. Purple at hue 284°, S 0.73, V 0.72. Pink at hue 323°, S 0.61, V 0.92 — uniquely bright and pastel. The mean and median nearly coincide for all colors except pink, which has bimodality from the ~0°/360° wrap-around.

data_table.description: Median HSV of displayed hexes per top-5 name

ana_11.label: Hue ranges (5th–95th percentile) per top-5 name
ana_11.content: The 5th-to-95th-percentile hue range covers each name's working territory. Brown spans hues 8–91° (a wide warm wedge), green 74–158°, blue 178–257°, purple 252–327°, and pink 15–352° (because pink wraps around the 0°/360° boundary). Adjacent names overlap slightly at boundaries: brown→green at ~75°, green→blue at ~160°, blue→purple at ~255°, purple→pink at ~325°, pink→brown at ~15°. These boundary regions are where naming disagreement is highest in subsequent analyses.

ana_12.label: Hue × name distribution — the rainbow as named territory
ana_12.content: Binning displayed hue into 10° bands and computing the within-band share of each top-5 name produces the canonical naming-territory plot. At hue 80–140° green dominates above 97%. At 180–230° blue is over 90%. Purple peaks around 280° (>95%). Pink owns 320–340° (over 90%). The transitions are sharp but real: at hue 50° brown gets 63% and green 35%; at 160° green is 67% and blue 32%. Around hue 0° pink and brown split ~48%/47% — the warm wrap-around where naming is most unstable.

ana_13.label: RGB-cube cell agreement — naming is mostly emphatic
ana_13.content: Binning displayed hex into a 12×12×12 RGB cube (1,728 cells, 612 answers per cell on average) and looking at the most-popular name per cell: 1,063 of 1,606 well-sampled cells (66.2%) have a winner with ≥90% share. 849 (52.9%) are at ≥95%. Only 14 cells (0.9%) drop below 50% winner share, and just 3 below 40%. The mean winner share across cells is 88.6%, median 95.8%. Color naming, in this top-5 vocabulary, is overwhelmingly *settled* across most of the RGB cube — the boundary regions are narrow.

ana_14.label: The most ambiguous cells — naming boundaries
ana_14.content: The 25 most ambiguous cells — winner share 33.9–50.8% — sit on the geometric boundaries between named regions. The single most contested cell, RGB ~(96,96,96) ('#606060', a true mid-grey), splits 33.9% purple, 25% brown, 23.2% blue, 16.1% green. Mid-grey gets *every* top-5 name: the brain has no anchor when nothing is saturated. Other contested cells include: '#b58a8a' (rose-grey: 35% purple / 32% pink / 31% brown), '#cab50a' (yellow-green: 45% green / 43% brown), and '#75f5ca' (cyan-green: 50% green / 49% blue). The list traces every border on the color wheel — the green/blue line at cyan, the blue/purple line at indigo, the pink/brown line at salmon, the purple/pink line at magenta.

ana_15.label: Most canonical cells per name — perfect-agreement exemplars
ana_15.content: At the centers of each named region, agreement is essentially total. For 'green', cells like RGB (10,176,10) (#0aa00a) and (10,181,10) (#0ab50a) get 100% green among 1,400+ answers each. Pure 'blue' cells like #0aa0e0 and #208ae0 reach 100% blue (n=805 and 977). For 'purple', #602060 reaches 99.6% purple. The most canonical 'pink' cell (#f58a8a) achieves 99.9%. The cleanest 'brown' (#a04a0a) hits 100% brown over 801 answers. These are the prototypical exemplars — RGB triples that the entire English-speaking xkcd readership names identically.

ana_16.label: Chromosome × naming divergence — small but real
ana_16.content: Across 1,560 well-sampled RGB-cube cells, the mean Manhattan-divergence between XY and XX naming distributions is only 0.040 (median 0.017, max 0.379). XY users say 'blue' for 26.42% of answers vs XX 28.59%; XY say 'green' 30.05% vs XX 28.90%. The aggregate gap is small (~1–2 percentage points). The largest cell-level XY-vs-XX divergence (0.378) is at #203535 — a dark teal-grey — where 68% of XY users said 'green' but 65% of XX said 'blue'. Other strongly-divergent cells are pink/purple/brown borderlands (#b50a4a, #e0b58a, #b5a0a0) where XX users converge harder on a single name while XY users spread answers more evenly. The pattern is consistent with prior linguistic research: XX users use color terms with higher in-group agreement at the same boundaries.

ana_17.label: Aggregate name share — XY vs XX
ana_17.content: Looking at all clean answers (spam_prob<0.5): XY users are 2.17 percentage points more likely to say 'blue' (XY 26.42% vs XX 28.59%), 1.14 pp less likely to say 'green', 0.73 pp less likely to say 'purple', 0.44 pp less likely to say 'brown'. XX users are slightly more likely to say 'pink' (12.51% vs 12.36%, +0.15 pp). The biggest single-name difference is 2.17 pp on 'blue' — this is consistent with prior research showing women have more granular blue/green discrimination, leading them to apply 'blue' to colors XY users would call 'green' or 'purple'.

data_table.description: Aggregate share of each top-5 name by chromosome (%)

ana_18.label: Spam probability is concentrated and skewed XY
ana_18.content: Mean spam_prob is 0.218 for XY users vs 0.162 for XX, despite identical medians (0.030). The high tail is the asymmetry: 7.40% of XY users have spam_prob > 0.5 vs 4.59% of XX. Within high-spam buckets the XY share rises dramatically — among spam_prob > 0.75, 81.5% of users are XY (vs the baseline ~71% XY share). Among spam_prob 0.5–0.75, 79.2% are XY. This empirically validates Munroe's 2010 anecdote that crude/joke entries skewed male. It also means any chromosome-conditional naming finding must include spam filtering as a robustness check.

data_table.description: % of users who are XY within each spam-prob bucket

ana_19.label: Colorblind users disagree on naming much more than non-colorblind
ana_19.content: The cell-level mean Manhattan-divergence between colorblind and non-colorblind answer distributions is 0.117 (median 0.065) — almost three times the chromosome divergence (0.040). Aggregate: colorblind users say 'green' 32.16% (vs 29.55% for non-colorblind, +2.62 pp), 'pink' 15.60% (vs 12.24%, +3.36 pp), 'purple' just 17.99% (vs 23.93%, -5.94 pp). The biggest cell-level divergence is at #b5a0ca (a soft lilac): colorblind users called it 'pink' 56.5% of the time while non-colorblind users called it 'purple' 87.4%. The pattern is consistent with red-green color blindness compressing the perceptual distance between purple and pink (both with red-channel components) — colorblind users substitute 'pink' where non-colorblind see 'purple'.

ana_20.content: The single most divergent cell, #b5a0ca (soft lilac), has colorblind users naming it 'pink' (57%) while non-colorblind name it 'purple' (87%) — a 0.70 Manhattan divergence. ana_21.label: Monitor type: small but visible effect on pink/green balance
ana_21.content: Aggregate naming on LCDs vs CRTs shows a consistent pattern: LCD users say 'pink' 12.50% of the time vs CRT users 10.21% (a 2.29 pp gap), and CRT users say 'green' 32.67% vs LCD's 29.58% (3.09 pp). 'Brown' is also more common on CRTs (8.53% vs 7.13%). The signature: CRTs render colors slightly warmer/dimmer (phosphor characteristics), so pinks tend to read as reds or browns, greens look more saturated. The differences are smaller than chromosome differences but cleanly directional.

data_table.description: Aggregate share of each top-5 name by monitor (%)

ana_22.label: The fuchsia/magenta line — pink-purple boundary
ana_22.content: The hue range 290–340° is where 'pink' and 'purple' contend for naming territory. At hue 280° purple owns 95.4%; at 300° purple still leads (88.2%) but pink jumps to 11.0%. By 320° pink is at 69.0% and purple just 30.5%. The boundary is at roughly hue 310°. Within this 290–340° wedge sit 'fuchsia' (often quoted hex #ff00ff at hue 300°), 'magenta' (xkcd hex #c20078 at hue 322°), and 'pink' itself. The dataset's quantitative answer: at the canonical magenta hex region, *people are split roughly 70/30 pink/purple*, validating Munroe's observation that fuchsia-magenta naming is unsettled — and also resolving it: at this hue, more people say pink than purple by a roughly 2-to-1 margin.

ana_23.label: Population colorblindness ratio benchmark mismatch
ana_23.content: Adjusted population estimates put red-green colorblindness at ~8% of XY individuals and ~0.5% of XX (a ~16x ratio). The xkcd dataset shows 4.99% in XY and 1.085% in XX — a 4.6x ratio. Even after stripping spam (spam<0.1) the ratio is only 4.77x, well short of the population value. This suggests strong selection bias on both sides: XX users who are color-curious are more likely to self-report colorblindness (a soft form of color sensitivity), and many XY users with mild color vision deficiency may not consider themselves 'colorblind' for survey purposes. The implication for color-naming research: the xkcd colorblind subsample is substantially less colorblind, in absolute terms, than a true population sample would be — yet the naming differences observed in ana_19 are still robust.

ana_24.label: Boundary regions are narrow but everywhere
ana_24.content: Of 1,606 well-sampled RGB-cube cells, only 14 (0.87%) have winner share below 50% and 60 (3.74%) are between 50-60%. Combined: ~4.6% of well-sampled cells qualify as 'naming boundaries'. These boundaries cluster predictably: along the green/blue line near hue 165° (cyan), along the purple/blue line near hue 250-260° (indigo/violet), along the purple/pink line near 310-320°, and through the achromatic core near (96,96,96). In total, the share of the displayed-color experience that is ambiguous is small but topologically well-distributed — every named region has its frontier.

data_table.description: Cumulative cells by winner-share threshold

ana_25.label: The full 949-color palette is a proxy English color lexicon
ana_25.content: The published 949 colors function as an empirical English color lexicon. Each color has a hex, rank, and HSV triple. The palette is biased toward yellow-green (152 yellows, 81 yellow-greens, 133 greens) and away from the saturated purple wedge (47). Brightness V averages 0.66 across all 949 — moderately bright, with very few dark colors. Saturation S averages 0.58, with strong bimodality (deep saturated names vs the muted/dusty/pale modifier family).

caveats.content: answers.csv is a *filtered* subset retaining only those answers where the user typed one of the top-5 most popular color names ('purple','green','blue','pink','brown'). Any analysis describes naming behavior within this restricted vocabulary, not over the full ~5M-response open vocabulary.
Each displayed hex was shown to at most ~5 different users (most are unique). Per-displayed-hex agreement cannot be measured; analyses bin to RGB-cube cells (12×12×12) or hue bins.
color_ranks.csv has 949 rows, not the round 954 sometimes quoted in xkcd's blog post — the TidyTuesday cleaning may have dropped some near-duplicates.
Spam and chromosome are entangled: 81% of users with spam_prob > 0.75 are XY. Always report chromosome findings with at least two spam thresholds.

The colorblindness ratio in this sample (XY/XX = 4.6x) is far below the population benchmark (~16x). The xkcd subsample is therefore not representative of population colorblindness, even though the *naming differences* observed in this subsample are robust.
